name: Pine Green
lede: Pine Green is a deep bluish green named after the conifer; the books say almost nothing about it as a color, but one jeweller's note shows where the word shows up in practice: amber.

sections.title: The name and the swatch
sections.body: Pine Green belongs to the plant-and-landscape names, and the swatch here matches RAL 6028, a screen approximation [2]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 files this color under strong bluish green, and the word's earliest record in our sources is the RAL list of 1927 [2]. That makes it a twentieth-century paint-card name, not an old pigment name [2]. Its parent family is [[green]], and it sits next to [[teal]] in hue [2].

sections.title: Green amber
sections.body: In Finlay's chapter on jewels, pine-green amber is popular in jewelry yet usually signals that the piece has been baked in an oven, above all when it holds sparkles [1]. She adds that treatments of all kinds are a growing problem in the amber trade, so a green stone calls for caution [1]. Blue [[amber]] is rare, and black is rarer still, usually because it has been artificially colored [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Pine Green is rare in painting: it appears in 0.03% of the archive (8 paintings), rarer than 79% of the named colors, as photographed [3]. Its first appearance is a painting of 1790, long before the name's 1927 record, so that match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment [3].
